Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: For which type of business organization is the Single Entry System considered most suitable?
Option A: Small size business concerns with a limited number of transactions
Option B: Large multinational corporations with thousands of daily transactions
Hint: Think about the size of the business and its transaction volume.
Explanation: The Single Entry System is generally suited to small businesses with relatively few transactions. Large multinational corporations usually need more complete accounting records.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which classes of accounts are completely omitted or not maintained under the Single Entry System?
Option A: Personal accounts of creditors and debtors
Hint: Recall which account classes are omitted in this system.
Explanation: Real and Nominal accounts are generally not maintained under the Single Entry System. Personal accounts of debtors and creditors are commonly kept.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Single Entry System is described in the text as an unsystematic combination of which of the following?
Option A: Double entry, Triple entry, and Reverse entry
Option B: Single entry, Double entry, and No Entry
Hint: Recall the types of entry combined in this system.
Explanation: The Single Entry System is an unsystematic combination of single entry, double entry, and no entry. Triple entry and reverse entry are not the stated combination.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What is a Statement of Affairs?
Option A: A statement of Assets and Liabilities prepared under the Single Entry System
Option B: A statement of all cash receipts and payments during a financial year
Hint: Think of the information a Statement of Affairs presents.
Explanation: A Statement of Affairs lists assets and liabilities under the Single Entry System. A statement of cash receipts and payments records cash movements instead.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In the format of a Statement of Affairs, which items are recorded on the left-hand side and right-hand side, respectively?
Option A: Left-hand side records Assets; Right-hand side records Liabilities
Option B: Left-hand side records Liabilities; Right-hand side records Assets
Hint: Recall how assets and liabilities are arranged in the statement.
Explanation: In a Statement of Affairs, liabilities appear on the left and assets on the right. Reversing these sides gives the wrong arrangement.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following items appears on the Liabilities side of a Statement of Affairs?
Hint: Identify which item represents an amount owed by the business.
Explanation: A bank overdraft is a liability because the business owes money to the bank. Prepaid expenses are assets.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Which of the following items appears on the Assets side of a Statement of Affairs?
Hint: Look for an expense paid before it is used up.
Explanation: Prepaid expenses are assets because they provide future economic benefit. A bank loan is a liability.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: What are the two recognized methods of calculating profit or loss when books are maintained under Single Entry, as noted in the text?
Option A: Net Worth Method and Conversion Method
Option B: Cash Flow Method and Fund Flow Method
Hint: Recall the two methods used to find profit or loss.
Explanation: The Net Worth Method and Conversion Method are the two recognized methods. Cash Flow and Fund Flow methods serve different purposes.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In the Net Worth Method, before accounting for adjustments, what indicates a Profit?
Option A: Closing Capital is more than Opening Capital
Option B: Closing Capital is equal to Opening Capital
Hint: Compare the opening and closing capital balances.
Explanation: Closing capital greater than opening capital indicates a profit before adjustments. Equal balances alone do not indicate an increase in capital.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How is Additional Capital treated in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Option A: It is added to Closing Capital
Option B: It is deducted from Closing Capital
Hint: Consider how new owner investment affects closing capital.
Explanation: Additional capital is deducted from closing capital when calculating profit, because it is an owner contribution rather than earned profit. Adding it would inflate the result.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: In what forms can Drawings be made by a proprietor as presented in the format of Statement of Profit or Loss?
Hint: Recall the forms in which an owner may withdraw value.
Explanation: Drawings may be made in cash or in kind. They are not limited to bank cheques.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How is Depreciation on fixed assets treated in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Option A: It is added as an income and gain
Option B: It is deducted as an expense and loss
Hint: Think of depreciation as a cost of using fixed assets.
Explanation: Depreciation is deducted as an expense or loss. It is not income or a gain.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: Where does Reserve for Doubtful Debts (R.D.D.) appear in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Option A: Under Expenses and Losses (to be deducted)
Option B: Under Incomes and Gains (to be added)
Hint: Recall where doubtful-debt reserves are treated in profit calculation.
Explanation: Reserve for Doubtful Debts is treated under expenses and losses and deducted. It is not an income or gain.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How is Interest on Capital treated in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Hint: Consider whether interest on the owner’s capital is a business cost.
Explanation: Interest on Capital is deducted under Expenses and Losses in the Statement of Profit or Loss. It is not added as income.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How is Interest on Drawings treated in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Option A: Added as an income to the business
Hint: Think about who benefits when interest is charged on drawings.
Explanation: Interest on Drawings is income to the business and is added. It is not an operating expense.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How are Outstanding (unpaid) Expenses treated in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Hint: Recall how unpaid expenses affect the year’s profit.
Explanation: Outstanding expenses are deducted under Expenses and Losses because they relate to the accounting period. They are not added as income.

Subject: Book-Keeping and Accountancy
Question: How are Prepaid Expenses (Unexpired Expenses) treated in the Statement of Profit or Loss?
Option A: Added in the Statement of Profit or Loss
Hint: Think about expenses paid now for a future period.
Explanation: Prepaid expenses are added back in the Statement of Profit or Loss because they do not belong to the current period’s expenses. They are not deducted as current expenses.
